source_text: μαίων αὐτῶν, καὶ εἰ ἐπαφῷτό τις μόνον, ἀκάθαρτον ἔσεσθαί φησιν, οὔτε, τὸν μετασχόντα τῆς ἐκείνων νεκρότητος, μώμου καὶ γραφῆς ἀπαλλάττων, οὔτε μὴν ἀναίτιον εἶναι λέγων, καὶ εἰ ἀγχοῦ τις ἴοι καὶ πλησιαζόμενος. Χρῆναι γὰρ οἶμαι νηφαλέως ἀποφοιτᾷν, οὐχὶ δήπου μόνης τῆς πρὸς φαύλους ταυτοεργίας, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ συνιέναι μόνον. «Ὁ γὰρ ἁπτόμενος πίσσης, μολυνθήσεται,» φησί. Καὶ ἀληθὴς ὁ λόγος· ὅτι δὲ εἰς ἠθῶν ποιότητα τὰ ἐκ τῶν παραδειγμάτων χρήσιμα τῷ νόμῳ παρείληπται, ἀναμάθοι τις ἂν ἐκ τῶν ἐπενηνεγμένων. Ἔφη γὰρ πάλιν· «Καὶ οὐ μὴ βδελύξεσθε τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἑρπετοῖς τοῖς ἕρπουσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, καὶ οὐ μιανθήσεσθε ἐν τούτοις, καὶ οὐκ ἀκάθαρτοι ἔσεσθε ἐν αὐτοῖς, ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῶν.» Ὁποῖον γὰρ ἂν ἐποίησε μολυσμὸν τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ψυχῇ, τὸ ἐκτεθνάναι ζῶον, καὶ τοῦ τεθνεῶτος ἀποθίγειν; Τί γὰρ ἂν ἠδίκησε βρῶσις, ἡ εἰς κοιλίαν χωροῦσα καὶ ἐκπεμπομένη πρὸς ἀφεδρῶνα, κατὰ τὴν τοῦ Σωτῆρος φωνήν; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Οὐδὲν, ὡς ἐγῷμαι· νοεῖς γὰρ ὀρθῶς. {ΚΥΡ.} Χρῆναι δὴ οὖν ἔγωγέ φημι, κατὰ τοὺς τῶν πλωτήρων εὐτεχνεστάτους, πάντα σείοντας κάλων, ἔξω φέρεσθαι μολυσμῶν, ἠρεμαῖαν δὲ ὥσπερ ἀκτὴν καὶ ἀκύμονα πρὸς τὴν Θεῷ φιλαιτάτην εἰσελαύνειν ζωήν. Προσιτὸς γὰρ ἡμῖν οὐχ ἑτέρως ἢ οὕτως ἂν γένοιτο καὶ μόνως, ἀληθὲς δὲ ὅτι τὸ χρῆμά ἐστιν, ἀταλαίπωρον ἰδεῖν. Γέγραπται γὰρ πάλιν ἐν τῇ Ἐξόδῳ· «Καὶ Μωσῆς ἦν ποιμαίνων τὰ πρόβατα Ἰοθὸρ τοῦ γαμβροῦ αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἱερέως Μαδιὰμ, καὶ ἤγαγε τὰ πρόβατα ὑπὸ τὴν ἔρημον· καὶ ἦλθεν εἰς τὸ ὅρος Χωρήβ. Ὤφθη δὲ αὐτῷ ἄγγελος Κυρίου ἐν πυρὶ φλογὸς ἐκ τοῦ βάτου, καὶ ὁρᾷ ὅτι ὁ βάτος καίεται πυρὶ, ὁ δὲ βάτος οὐ κατεκαίετο. Εἶπε δὲ Μωσῆς· Παρελθὼν ὄψομαι τὸ ὅραμα τὸ μέγα τοῦτο, ὅτι οὐ κατακαίεται ὁ βάτος. Ὡς δὲ εἶδε Κύριος ὅτι προσάγει ἰδεῖν, ἐκάλεσεν αὐτὸν ὁ Κύριος ἐκ τοῦ βάτου, λέγων· Μωσῆ, Μωσῆ· ὁ δὲ εἶπε· Τί ἐστιν; Ὁ δὲ εἶπε· Μὴ ἐγγίσῃς ὧδε, λύσαι τὸ ὑπόδημα ἐκ τῶν ποδῶν σου· ὁ γὰρ τόπος, ἐν ᾧ σὺ ἕστηκας, γῆ ἁγία ἐστί.» Συνίης οὖν ὅπως οὐκ ἂν ἀγχοῦ γένοιτό τις τοῦ πανάγνου Θεοῦ, μὴ οὐχὶ πάντα ῥύπον τῆς ἑαυτοῦ προαπονίζων ψυχῆς· νεκρότητος δὲ ἁπάσης τῆς ὡς ἐν πράγμασι νοουμένης, ἀπολύων τὸν πόδα, τοῦτ' ἔστι, τὴν εἰς τὰ πρακτέα βάδισιν νοητήν; Ἢ γὰρ οὐχὶ τὸ ὑπόδημα, νεκροῦ ζώου λείψανον; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πῶς γὰρ οὔ; {ΚΥΡ.} Τύπος οὖν ἄρα νεκρότητος τὸ χρῆμά ἐστιν, ἣν εἴπερ τις ἀποφορτίσαιτο, τὰ δι' ὧν ἂν ἐξοίχοιτο διαῤῥήξας δεσμὰ, ἥξει τε ἀγχοῦ καὶ οἰκεῖος ἔσται Θεῷ, καὶ πρός γε τὸ σώζειν ἑτέρους δύνασθαι λοιπὸν, ἐπιτηδείως ἔχων. Προσεχειρίζετο γοῦν ὁ Μωσῆς εἰς ἀποστολὴν, καὶ πρὸς ἐκλύτρωσιν τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ. Ἱερὸς δὲ ἡμῖν ὑποπεφώνηκε λόγος· «Υἱὲ, ἐὰν σοφὸς γένῃ, σεαυτῷ σοφὸς ἔση καὶ τῷ πλησίον σου.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εὖ λέγεις.
pass_a_gloss: …[carcass]es of them, and if one only touch, he says will be unclean, neither releasing from blame and indictment the one sharing in their deadness, nor saying one is guiltless even if one goes near and approaches. For I think one must soberly depart not only from same-working with the base, but even from merely being together with them. [Sir 13:1: the one touching pitch will be defiled], it says. And the word is true. That the useful things from the examples were taken up by the law for the quality of morals, one could learn from what was added. For he said again: [Lev 11:43–44 LXX: you shall not make your souls abominable with all the creeping things creeping on the earth, and you will not be defiled in these, and not be unclean in them, because I am the Lord your God]. For what sort of defilement would the dying of an animal, and touching the dead, make for the soul of man? For what would food harm, going into the belly and sent out to the drain/privy, according to the voice of the Saviour? PALL. Nothing, as I think; for you understand rightly. CYR. I say then one must, according to the most skilful of sailors, shaking every rope (proverb using every effort full sail), be carried out of defilements, and drive into the life most dear to God as into a calm and waveless shore. For [he] would become approachable to us not otherwise than thus and only; and that the matter is true is effortless to see. For it is written again in Exodus: [Exod 3:1–5 LXX: Moses was shepherding the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law, priest of Midian, and led the sheep under the wilderness, and came to the mountain Horeb; an angel of the Lord appeared to him in fire of flame out of the bush, and he sees the bush burns with fire but the bush was not burned up; Moses said: passing by I will see this great sight, that the bush is not burned up; when the Lord saw that he approaches to see, the Lord called him out of the bush: Moses, Moses; he said: What is it? He said: Do not draw near here; loose the sandal from your feet, for the place in which you stand is holy ground]. Do you understand then how one would not come near the all-pure God unless first washing off every filth of his own soul, and loosing the foot from all deadness understood as in deeds, that is, the mental/spiritual walking toward things to be done? For is not the sandal the remnant of a dead animal? PALL. How not? CYR. The thing then is a type of deadness, which if one should unload, having broken the bonds through which he would perish, he will come near and be one’s own to God, and be suitably disposed henceforth to be able to save others too. Moses at any rate was appointed for sending out and for the redemption of the sons of Israel. A sacred word has declared to us: [Prov 9:12 LXX: Son, if you become wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbour]. PALL. You speak well.
pass_b_english: Cyril: …of their carcasses will be unclean, and so will anyone who only touches them. It does not free from blame and accusation the one who has shared in their deadness, nor does it call anyone guiltless even if he only comes close and draws near. For I think we must soberly keep away not only from doing the same deeds as the wicked, but even from merely keeping company with them. ‘For whoever touches pitch will be defiled,’ it says (Sirach 13:1). And the saying is true. That the law took up the lessons of these examples for the forming of character, one may learn from what follows. For it said again: ‘You shall not make your souls loathsome with any of the creeping things that creep on the earth, and you shall not be defiled by them, and you shall not be unclean through them; for I am the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 11:43–44). For what defilement could an animal’s dying, or touching what has died, bring upon the human soul? What harm could food do, which goes into the belly and is sent out into the drain, as the Savior said (Matthew 15:17)?
Palladius: None, I think; you understand it rightly.

Cyril: Then I say that we must, like the most skillful sailors, crowd on every sail and run clear of defilements, and put in to the life most dear to God as to a calm shore where no waves break. For God could become approachable to us in this way alone and in no other, and that this is true is easy to see. For it is written again in Exodus: ‘Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian, and he led the sheep into the wilderness and came to Mount Horeb. And an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the bush, and he saw that the bush was burning with fire, yet the bush was not consumed. And Moses said, “I will turn aside and see this great sight, why the bush is not consumed.” When the Lord saw that he was drawing near to look, the Lord called to him out of the bush, saying, “Moses, Moses.” And he said, “What is it?” And he said, “Do not come near here; take the sandal off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground”’ (Exodus 3:1–5). Do you see, then, that no one could come near the all-pure God without first washing every stain from his own soul, and freeing his foot from all the deadness that lies in deeds? By the foot I mean the spiritual walk by which we go toward what must be done. For is not the sandal the remains of a dead animal?

Cyril: Then the sandal is a type of deadness. If anyone throws off this deadness like a load and breaks the bonds that would be his ruin, he will come near and belong to God, and from then on he will be fit to save others as well. So it was that Moses was appointed to be sent out, and to redeem the sons of Israel. And a sacred saying has told us: ‘Son, if you become wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbor’ (Proverbs 9:12).

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 14 exists to compare. Translated fresh from the Migne PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

Opens mid-word (‘…μαίων αὐτῶν’), completing ‘the one who eats of their carcasses’ from sec. 26 (Leviticus 11:40, already cited there). ‘For whoever touches pitch will be defiled’ is Sirach 13:1 (LXX ὁ ἁπτόμενος πίσσης μολυνθήσεται), cited by its English name Sirach. ‘You shall not make your souls loathsome’ follows LXX Leviticus 11:43 (Cyril reads βδελύξεσθε for the LXX’s βδελύξητε; same sense). The Saviour’s saying about food going into the belly and out into the drain is Matthew 15:17 (εἰς ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται); Mark 7:19 is parallel but uses different wording, so only Matthew is cited. ‘Crowd on every sail’ renders the proverb πάντα κάλων σείειν (‘shake out every rope’, to use every effort); the participle σείοντας belongs to ‘we’, not to the sailors, so the English makes us the ones who set sail. Προσιτὸς has no expressed subject; God is supplied from the sense and the following Exodus proof. LXX ὑπὸ τὴν ἔρημον rendered ‘into the wilderness’; ‘Παρελθὼν ὄψομαι’ rendered ‘I will turn aside and see’ (literally ‘passing by’). Proverbs 9:12 is quoted in its LXX form (‘Son… and for your neighbour’), which differs from the Hebrew-based English but has the same verse number. ‘So it was that Moses was appointed’ renders γοῦν with imperfect προσεχειρίζετο; ‘to redeem’ renders εἰς… ἐκλύτρωσιν. νοητήν (of the ‘walk’) rendered ‘spiritual’, Cyril’s usual contrast with the bodily foot. ἥν (‘which if one unloads’) refers to νεκρότητος, so ‘throws off this deadness like a load’ names the referent.
ἣν ... ἀποφορτίσαιτο: referent made explicit ('throws off this deadness like a load')
Scripture checked: Sirach 13:1, Lev 11:43-44 LXX, Matthew 15:17 (εἰς ἀφεδρῶνα ἐκβάλλεται), Exodus 3:1-5 LXX, Proverbs 9:12 LXX all match their cited verses
